summary: Moses Isserles of Krakow (the Rema, c. 1530-1572) is recorded in the tradition as the preeminent Ashkenazi halakhic authority of the sixteenth century. His glosses on Joseph Karo's Shulchan Aruch, collectively titled the Mappah ('the Tablecloth'), recorded Ashkenazi custom (minhag) where it diverged from Karo's largely Sephardic rulings, and the combined work, Karo's 'Set Table' with Isserles' 'Tablecloth', came to be regarded across both major branches of the Jewish world as the authoritative code of Jewish law.
description:
Moses Isserles (c. 1530-1572), known by the acronym the Rema (ReMA, Rabbi Moshe Isserles), was a rabbi and halakhic authority in Krakow, where he headed a yeshiva and served on the rabbinical court. The tradition records him as the leading posek of Ashkenazi Jewry in his generation, the counterpart in the Ashkenazi world to Joseph Karo (1488-1575) in the Sephardic. This entry presents his standing and his rulings as attributed features of his work and of the tradition's regard for it, not as claims the editor affirms.

Isserles' principal halakhic project began as an independent one. He composed the Darkei Moshe ('the Ways of Moses'), a commentary on the Arbaah Turim (the 'Tur') of Jacob ben Asher, tracing the law and its authorities much as Karo had done in his own Tur-commentary, the Beit Yosef. When Karo's Beit Yosef and then his digest the Shulchan Aruch appeared, Isserles recast his work: rather than issue a competing code, he wrote glosses to be printed alongside Karo's text, recording where Ashkenazi practice and the later authorities (the Acharonim) differed from the rulings Karo had drawn from the largely Sephardic tradition. These glosses, printed interwoven with the Shulchan Aruch from the Krakow editions onward, are collectively titled the Mappah ('the Tablecloth'), set over Karo's 'Set Table'. Through them the combined work spoke to both branches of practice at once, the base text carrying Karo's ruling and the gloss the Ashkenazi, and it came in the reception of the tradition to be treated as the authoritative code of halakha across both communities.

A guiding principle attributed to Isserles is deference to established Ashkenazi custom (minhag Ashkenaz) and to the later authorities where they had settled a practice: where Karo followed his pillars among the earlier authorities (Alfasi, Maimonides, and Asher ben Yehiel), Isserles frequently ruled with the minhag and the Acharonim as received among Ashkenazim. The character of his glossing can be seen in the very first ruling of the code. To Karo's opening charge at Orach Chayim 1:1, that one should 'strengthen himself like a lion to get up in the morning to serve his creator', Isserles' opening Hagah (gloss) adds the verse 'I have set the Lord always before me' (shiviti, Psalm 16:8), calling it 'a great principle in the Torah and among the virtues of the righteous who walk before God', and it develops the theme of the constant awareness of God with reference to Maimonides' Guide of the Perplexed (III:52). This gloss, read line-by-line on the open text of Sefaria, is the openly-auditable primary that carries Isserles' authorship of the Mappah and its function in his own words.

Isserles' relationship to Karo is recorded as complementary and divergent at once: the scholarship records no personal meeting between the two, though they corresponded on halakhic questions, and Isserles' glosses both complete Karo's code for the Ashkenazi reader and mark, siman by siman, where Ashkenazi ruling parts from the Sephardic base text. The difference in the two rulings, Sephardic in the base and Ashkenazi in the gloss, is described here as a difference of received practice between communities, not ranked or adjudicated by the editor. Isserles was also a student of philosophy and kabbalah and wrote beyond halakha, but he is remembered above all as the author of the Mappah, the layer that made Karo's Shulchan Aruch a code for the whole Jewish world.
editorial_notes: This entry presents Moses Isserles (the Rema, c. 1530-1572) on Judaism's own terms as the preeminent Ashkenazi halakhic authority of the sixteenth century, author of the Darkei Moshe (his commentary on the Tur) and above all of the Mappah glosses on Karo's Shulchan Aruch, and his principle of following minhag Ashkenaz and the later authorities (neutrality #1, #4, #7). lifespan.note: c. 1530-1572 CE (the birth year is given approximately in the scholarship, commonly c. 1525-1530). Lived and taught in Krakow (Cracow), in the Polish-Lithuanian realm, where he headed a yeshiva and served on the rabbinical court; the leading Ashkenazi halakhic authority of his generation.
